danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 22
paragraphs: Imidlertid var selve byen øde. Der var næsten ingen på gaderne. Porte og butikker var alle lukket, kun hist og her omkring værtshusene hørtes enkelte råb eller berusede sange. Ingen kørte gennem gaderne, og der hørtes sjældent fodtrin. Povarskajagaden var ganske stille og øde. Rostov-familiens store gård var oversået med strå og hestegødning, og der var ikke en sjæl at se. I den store dagligstue, der var blevet efterladt med alt sit indhold, var der to mennesker. Det var gårdsportieren Ignat og pagen Misjka, Vasilitjs barnebarn, der var blevet i Moskva hos sin bedstefar. Misjka havde åbnet klavichordiet og klimprede på det med én finger. Gårdsportieren stod med armene i siden og smilede tilfreds foran det store spejl.
»Er det ikke fint, hva, onkel Ignat?« sagde drengen og begyndte pludselig at hamre løs på klaviaturet med begge hænder.
»Nå da!« svarede Ignat, overrasket over det bredere grin, der viste sig i spejlet.

»Frækhed! Frækhed!« hørte de bag sig stemmen af Mavra Kuzminitjna, der var kommet lydløst ind. »Sikke han griner, det fede fjæs! Er det det, du er her for? Der er ikke ryddet op dernede, og Vasilij er udslidt. Vent bare du!«
Ignat holdt op med at smile, rettede på sit bælte og gik ud af værelset med ydmygt sænket blik.
»Tante, jeg gjorde det forsigtigt,« sagde drengen.
»Jeg skal give dig forsigtigt, din abekat!« udbrød Mavra Kuzminitjna og løftede armen truende. »Gå hen og sæt samovaren over til din bedstefar.«
Mavra Kuzminitjna børstede støvet af klavichordiet, lukkede det og forlod dagligstuen med et dybt suk og låste hoveddøren.
Ude i gården standsede hun for at overveje, hvor hun skulle gå hen — ind at drikke te i tyendets fløj hos Vasilij eller ind i forrådskammeret for at lægge det på plads, der stadig lå fremme.
Hun hørte lyden af hurtige fodtrin i den stille gade. Nogen standsede ved porten, og klinken raslede, da nogen forsøgte at åbne den. Mavra Kuzminitjna gik hen til porten.
»Hvem søger De?«
»Greven — grev Ilja Andrejevitj Rostov.«
»Og hvem er De?«
»En officer, jeg skal tale med ham,« lød svaret med en behagelig, veldannet russisk stemme.
Mavra Kuzminitjna åbnede porten, og en officer på atten år med Rostov-familiens runde ansigt trådte ind i gården.
»De er rejst, min herre. Rejste i går ved aftenstid,« sagde Mavra Kuzminitjna hjerteligt.
Den unge officer, der stod i porten og tøvede med at gå ind eller ej, klaskede med tungen.
»Åh, hvor ærgerligt!« mumlede han. »Jeg skulle være kommet i går... Hvor ærgerligt.«
Mavra Kuzminitjna betragtede imidlertid opmærksomt og medfølende den unge mands velkendte Rostov-ansigtstræk, hans slidte frakke og nedtrådte støvler.
»Hvad ville De tale med greven om?« spurgte hun.
»Nå ja... det kan ikke hjælpes!« sagde han i en ærgerlig tone og lagde hånden på porten, som for at gå.
Han standsede igen i ubeslutsomhed.

»Forstår De,« sagde han pludselig, »jeg er i familie med greven, og han har været meget venlig mod mig. Som De kan se« — han kiggede med et fornøjet og godmodigt smil på sin frakke og sine støvler — »er mit tøj slidt, og jeg har ingen penge, så jeg ville bede greven...«
Mavra Kuzminitjna lod ham ikke tale færdig.
»Vent bare et øjeblik, min herre. Ét lille øjeblik,« sagde hun.
Så snart officeren slap portgrebet, vendte hun om, og så hurtigt hendes gamle ben kunne bære hende, skyndte hun sig gennem baggården til tyendefløjen.

Mens Mavra Kuzminitjna løb hen til sit værelse, gik officeren rundt i gården og betragtede sine slidte støvler med sænket blik og et svagt smil på læberne. »Sikken ærgerligt, at jeg er gået glip af onkel! Sikken rar gammel kone! Hvor mon hun løb hen? Og hvordan finder jeg den korteste vej til at indhente mit regiment, der nu må være tæt på Rogozjskij-porten?« tænkte han. Netop da dukkede Mavra Kuzminitjna op bag hushjørnet med et forskrækket, men beslutsomt udtryk og et sammenrullet ternet tørklæde i hånden. Mens hun endnu var et par skridt fra officeren, foldede hun tørklædet ud, tog en hvid femogtyverubelsseddel ud af det og rakte den hastigt til ham.
»Hvis hans excellence havde været hjemme, ville han som en slægtning naturligvis... men som det er...«
Mavra Kuzminitjna blev forlegen og forvirret. Officeren afslog ikke, men tog stille sedlen og takkede hende.
»Hvis greven havde været hjemme...« gentog Mavra Kuzminitjna undskyldende. »Kristus være med Dem, min herre! Gud bevare Dem!« sagde hun og nejede, da hun fulgte ham ud.
Den unge officer, der rystede på hovedet og smilede, som morede han sig over sig selv, løb næsten i trav gennem de øde gader hen mod Jauzabroen for at indhente sit regiment.

Men Mavra Kuzminitjna stod ved den lukkede port et stykke tid med fugtige øjne, tankefuldt rystende på hovedet og følende en uventet strøm af moderlig ømhed og medlidenhed med den ukendte unge officer.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 22
paragraphs: Meanwhile the city itself was deserted. There was hardly anyone in the streets. The gates and shops were all shut; only here and there near taverns could solitary shouts or drunken songs be heard. Nobody drove through the streets, and footsteps were rare. Povarskaya Street was perfectly still and empty. The huge courtyard of the Rostov house was littered with wisps of hay and horse manure, and not a soul was in sight. In the great drawing room of the house — left with everything in it — were two people: the yard porter Ignat and the page boy Mishka, Vasilich's grandson, who had stayed behind in Moscow with his grandfather. Mishka had opened the clavichord and was picking out a tune with one finger. The yard porter, arms akimbo, stood smiling with satisfaction before the large mirror.
"Isn't it great, Uncle Ignat?" said the boy, suddenly banging the keyboard with both hands.
"Well I never!" Ignat replied, amazed at the broadening grin on his face in the mirror.

"Shameless! Shameless!" came the voice of Mavra Kuzminichna, who had entered silently. "Look at him grinning, the fat mug! Is that what you're here for? Nothing's been cleaned up downstairs and Vasilich is worn out. Just you wait!"
Ignat stopped smiling, adjusted his belt, and left the room with meekly downcast eyes.
"Auntie, I was doing it gently," said the boy.
"I'll give you gently, you monkey!" cried Mavra Kuzminichna, raising her arm threateningly. "Go start the samovar for your grandfather."
Mavra Kuzminichna flicked the dust off the clavichord and closed it, and with a deep sigh left the drawing room, locking the main door behind her.
Going out into the yard, she paused to consider where to go next — to the servants' wing for tea with Vasilich, or to the storeroom to put away what still lay about.
She heard the sound of quick footsteps in the quiet street. Someone stopped at the gate and the latch rattled as they tried to open it. Mavra Kuzminichna went to the gate.
"Who do you want?"
"The count — Count Ilya Andreevich Rostov."
"And who are you?"
"An officer. I need to see him," came the reply in a pleasant, well-bred Russian voice.
Mavra Kuzminichna opened the gate, and an officer of about eighteen, with the round face of a Rostov, entered the yard.
"They've gone away, sir. Left yesterday at vespers," Mavra Kuzminichna said warmly.
The young officer, standing in the gateway as if undecided whether to enter, clicked his tongue.
"How annoying!" he muttered. "I should have come yesterday. What a shame."
Meanwhile, Mavra Kuzminichna was studying with attention and sympathy the familiar Rostov features in the young man's face, his tattered coat and worn-down boots.
"What did you want to see the count for?" she asked.
"Oh well, it can't be helped!" he said in a vexed tone, placing his hand on the gate as if to leave.
He paused again, undecided.

"You see," he said suddenly, "I'm a relative of the count's, and he's been very kind to me. As you can see" — he glanced with an amused, good-natured smile at his coat and boots — "my things are worn out and I have no money, so I was going to ask the count..."
Mavra Kuzminichna didn't let him finish.
"Just wait a moment, sir. One little moment," she said.
And as soon as the officer let go of the gate handle, she turned and — hurrying on her old legs — went through the back yard to the servants' quarters.

While Mavra Kuzminichna was running to her room, the officer walked about the yard, looking down at his worn-out boots with a faint smile. "What a shame I missed Uncle! What a nice old woman! Where has she run off to? And how do I find the shortest way to catch up with my regiment? It must be getting near the Rogozhsky gate by now," he thought. Just then Mavra Kuzminichna appeared from behind the corner of the house, looking frightened but resolute, carrying a rolled-up handkerchief. While still a few steps away, she unfolded it, pulled out a white twenty-five-ruble banknote, and hastily pressed it into his hand.
"If his excellency had been at home — as a relative, naturally, he would have... but as things are..."
Mavra Kuzminichna grew flustered and confused. The officer didn't refuse but took the money quietly and thanked her.
"If the count had been at home..." Mavra Kuzminichna went on apologetically. "Christ be with you, sir! May God keep you safe!" she said, bowing as she saw him out.
Shaking his head and smiling, as if amused at himself, the officer ran nearly at a trot through the empty streets toward the Yauza bridge to catch up with his regiment.
But Mavra Kuzminichna stood at the closed gate for some time, her eyes moist, pensively shaking her head, feeling an unexpected surge of motherly tenderness and pity for the unknown young officer.
